body: I can't replicate this in a general project, can you replicate this in a completely new project yourself?

I can try, but is there like no easy bool variable somewhere in the engine to check the screen reader detection status? If I'm understanding what's going wrong correctly, then a blank project with nothing in it could also be used to check if the engine internally thinks there is a screen reader or not.

I can try to replicate the triggering condition in a new project, though it will take until next week as I'm making a new release of the game I'm working on for tomorrow so I can't spare any development time for this before that is out.
Since with these instructions alone I can't replicate the issue, so a minimal project or more specific instructions would be needed unfortunately, can't replicate unwanted focus in my own projects

According to the documentation on Control focus_mode property, the value of "Accessibility" which is the default now says: The online documentation doesn't seem to have this text: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.5/classes/class_control.html#class-control-property-focus-mode But that in-engine text very heavily implies that if a screen reader isn't detected, the node should be totally unable to grab focus. However it does, and I've confirmed that the few problematic instances so far I've noticed go away if I swap the mode to None. So based on the documentation the engine should be incorrectly thinking that there is an active screen reader. Thus I think that there is a bug in whatever code in the engine determines if a screen reader is active or not. To test that I think it would be sufficient to go into the Godot source code and just call something like `std::exit` if a screen reader is detected as active. That would make it very clear when Godot accidentally detects a screen reader.

`Accessibility` is not the default in general, did you set it manually? Or on what node are you seeing that focus mode? The default is `0`, or "None" for `Control`, and is `2`, or "All" for some other nodes like buttons

I did not set it manually, it seems to be the default for rich text labels which are so far the only GUI elements I've noticed the problem on. So it is possible the problem is only *visible* there.

But a detection of a screen reader being present when there isn't one can cause GUI problems for players in general in games that implement screen reader support as the changed visuals wouldn't correctly turn off when there is no screen reader.

Ah yes that one does have that as the default mode indeed, most don't, but I can't replicate this with a `RichTextLabel` on my end either with a minimal setup, so this might be specific to specific OS versions or something

So if you can create a minimal project for this showing the issue I can test it, but with just this I can't replicate it on my end

I'll get back to this next week once I have time to investigate. I'll likely start digging into the engine source code to see what the screen reader detection code looks like and if I can compile a custom engine variant that just crashes when it thinks there's a screen reader for easy testing.

Would be best to get an MRP first but any investigation of the code as well would be great!

Would have to be done to avoid creating false negatives though, that'd be more important than preventing false positives

Some Linux configs falsely reporting screen-reader status is a known issue, so far we were not able to determine exact cause, since it is never reproducible on the clean installs of the same distros. So it's not clear what might be causing it (most likely some software is abusing accessibility APIs). Currently used checks are already excessively strict.

I'd personally prefer a conservative approach (with an explicit way to force it on), as I do not want to receive a bunch of confusing bug reports from players with strange white squares over their screen after the Godot 4.5 upgrade, which didn't warn about this (or I skimmed that part of the release notes, if so, sorry): (screenshots from the original bug report that alerted me to this) Now that I know about the problem I can easily enough identify what's going on, but first time seeing that bug report it was extremely confusing how a part of the game that hadn't been touched at all could just suddenly break and at a first glance draw random white boxes on the player's screen.

For the reference, you can make the same check manually, by running the following commands:


```
dbus-send --dest=org.a11y.Bus --print-reply /org/a11y/bus org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties.Get string:org.a11y.Status string:IsEnabled
```
Indicate that screen reader is running (so should return `false` if it's not).

```
dbus-send --dest=org.a11y.Bus --print-reply /org/a11y/bus org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties.Get string:org.a11y.Status string:ScreenReaderEnabled
```
Indicate that screen reader is configured to automatically start on login (so should also return `false`).


> personally prefer a conservative approach (with an explicit way to force it on)

Disabling it by default, removing it will make RTLs invisible to the screen-reader, so it is not a reasonable option. But we do not need to draw the border if selection is disabled.

Also, you can fully disable accessibility support in the project settings if you want to.

This is the only checks used to detect screen reader. Please run the following GDScript code it your project to make sure it is actually screen-reader detection that is causing it:

```gdscript
print(DisplayServer.accessibility_screen_reader_active())
```
You can also set `focus` stylebox for `Label` and `RichTextLabel` in your project theme to `StyleBoxEmpty` to make it invisible.

Interestingly enough that prints 0. However, if I just change this one property, do absolutely nothing else and then restart my game and go to the relevant place in the game again, the white square is gone. Changing this one single property on a rich text label (it does have a few of our game customizations on it): After game restart: So that's why I think it is related to the new accessibility feature. I guess I need to try to make that minimal problematic example next week. Here's a commit where this problem is present: https://github.com/Revolutionary-Games/Thrive/commit/b258759636818d3b37128bbd3c9fde21a2980013 (though it is in no way minimal) Also I can set the project accessibility mode to off to also get rid of the problem everywhere at once. > You can also set focus stylebox for Label and RichTextLabel in your project theme to StyleBoxEmpty to make it invisible. There's a few cases in our GUI where keyboard navigation is implemented and labels need to have focus styles. So fixing this like that would result in having to go through the entire game GUI and checking everything which would take quite many hours. This would still make navigation flow not work correctly, right? In my second screenshot the correct button on the popup window is now selected by default instead of the text thanks to the property change.

If the accessibility mode returns false then it can't have to do with the detection though, so it has to be somewhere related to checking that

But a MRP would be needed to pin down the specifics, and make sure it's not a configuration error

> Interestingly enough that prints 0. However, if I just change this one property, do absolutely nothing else and then restart my game and go to the relevant place in the game again, the white square is gone.

`0` is disabled. In this case, it should be something else that is causing the issue, likely in the `RichTextLabel` itself. And disabling accessibility likely won't fix it. I will check it.

I could have sworn it worked before, but now setting the project accessibility mode to "Disabled" doesn't seem to fix it anymore...

So I guess for now I'll turn that engine setting back on and manually fix the few rich text labels I know for sure trigger the problem to have lower chance to get bug reports from players about this.

Might be related to `grab_focus` call somewhere (like one fixed in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111250) or in the project. It seems like `FOCUS_ACCESSIBILITY` allow `grab_focus` to work regardless of screen-reader state, which is a bug. At least this is the only route which can lead to an incorrect focus, I can see at the first glance.

It could be. So far all the problematic instances have been inside a window control. And due to how inflexible those were in Godot 3, we have a custom implementation on top for window handling and that might now need fixing, as I see we have a line of code like `if (control.FocusMode != Control.FocusModeEnum.None)` to do some handling.


Edit: it works with that! So the root cause of our problems was that our emulation of window opening trying to grab focus to the first node in a window (as this is what Godot does by default) was not updated to handle accessibility type focus modes, so it attempted and managed to force focus on the rich text labels. Adding a check that the mode is not none and not accessibility seems to fix everything neatly.

Thank you for digging deeper into it, this highlights the importance of making an MRP to figure out what a bug actually is, they aren't just for helping us pinpoint the specifics of the bug (like bisecting the bug, or testing different areas to figure out what might be causing it) or to confirm that a fix is correct and solves the problem (and unlike what many assume an MRP isn't really about "proving" that a bug exists)

But I've come across plenty of reports like this one where the actual cause of the issue is completely different from what was first assumed, and often those cases are figured out once an MRP is attempted when the author tests our and identifies what actual steps are required to replicate the bug

I myself figured out areas affected by a bug I was reporting recently by making the MRP, identifying that it affected nodes I didn't realize it affected from my original project where I identified the bug

Yeah definitely, investigating the initial symptoms often leads to an unexpected ultimate root cause. 

Unfortunately in my case most engine regressions or bugs that impact Thrive are only caught once we release a public test build one week before the release when a small fraction of our playerbase gets their hands on the new version. Usually that also means that any new features we've made are also not totally bug-free and need fixing. So often investigating engine bugs is the last thing on my priority list. I actually just meant to make a small reddit post highlighting how the new accessibility mode might be causing problems for other game devs as well (as I would have likely saved at least 2 hours if I had seen anyone talking about this), but I got a comment that highlighted how what I saw should not have been happening so I decided to open a "quick" issue about it as well. And well quick issues often turn out to not be actually so quick...

I'm actually in general very scared of modifying any enum as it can extremely easily lead to bugs like this. Which in this case hit both the engine and code written by me. Also it seems like the Godot source code is not taking advantage of enum classes and switch statements where compilers can automatically check all new enum values are handled, which seems pretty bad from a code maintenance viewpoint.

I just re-read the 4.5 release announcement and the porting guide and they make no mention whatsoever of this added enum value, which to me seems like it should have been highlighted as a source code incompatibility as any code that previously handled the other focus mode enum values has a very high chance to need updating to handle the new value.

Hopefully [#112251](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/112251) gets merged soon so that someone might be saved in the future from hours of tracking down what's going wrong and instead can be pointed to the actual bug (in their code) much faster with the new error message.

> Also it seems like the Godot source code is not taking advantage of enum classes and switch statements where compilers can automatically check all new enum values are handled, which seems pretty bad from a code maintenance viewpoint.

We generally handle this with compiler checks and similar, so this rarely causes any problems

The same goes for user code, it should make sure it handles all elements of the enum and catch cases where it fails to handle a new value

> We generally handle this with compiler checks and similar, so this rarely causes any problems

Interesting, which check is that? I've not written much C++ in recent years so if there's a new tool to help here I'd be interested to learn it.

It's a standard warning under higher c++ checks, it complains if an enum value hasn't been used in a switch statement, alternatively we add `default` cases with errors or dev asserts to catch the same
Oh nice, I thought that it only worked for enum classes but apparently it also works for plain enums as well. Good to know.
